memories.memory_text: I'm up on the platform inside the glass tower, moving quickly—there's no time to waste. The mirror-bright object is pulsing, and the red sun outside makes everything feel like it's burning.
I remember slamming the TV off and shouting at that fool newscaster—this wasn't some random cosmic accident, it was an attack, planned by a mind. I could feel the truth of it burning in my chest.
I pulled the the glass case on Morgan Vale when he hesitated—calmly, firmly. I had to make him understand: we were launching now, or Eastgate Street was finished.
I saw the red bolts striking the greenhouse, glass exploding—I shouted into the chaos, demanding Morgan Vale show himself or I’d shoot.
I had the the glass case aimed at Morgan Vale's back—he was just walking away, leaving us all to die—I shouted that I couldn't take it off alone, that if he wouldn't come, who else would I find?

I saw the recognition Tristan Hawthorne in Jonah Vale's eyes when she remembered me from that Crown Hill Medical Center article — the one that called me insane after I left NASA. I hesitated, then confirmed who I was, watching her try to backtrack her words.

I pointed the the glass case at Tristan Hawthorne and told them to go up the stairs ahead of me. The greenhouse was breaking apart from laser strikes and fire, and I urged them to move quickly. Eastgate Street was under attack — we had no time to waste.
I tore the foliage aside and revealed the black lantern—bright as a mirror, untouched by the storm—then yanked the door open and told them I’d shoot if they didn’t get in.
Jonah Vale was backing away, refusing, and Tristan Hawthorne was about to jump—so I shoved her hard, off-balance, into the black lantern before he could act.
I forced Tristan Hawthorne to the seat and shouted at him to put his foot on the red pedal—then he attacked me, but I twisted away and hit the switch just as I was falling.
The G-force crushed me against the wall, my face straining, barely able to speak—each word took everything: friendship, the world ending, and the three of us having to stop it.
I watched my Stonebridge Warehouse climb into the sky, spinning fast and untouched by their laser fire—each bolt glancing off like sparks against steel.
I saw Harborview Plaza's molten surface rushing toward us, a sea of amber fire, and I crawled to the controls—my hands shaking as I flipped switches, but nothing responded.
By God, we did it! We made it!
I don't know where we are.

I told Tristan Hawthorne to extend his hand—it’s the universal gesture of friendship—and seconds later, they slammed a manacle on his wrist and threw him down; they were capturing us, not greeting us.
I shouted 'You inhuman fiend!' after seeing that armored man throw himself onto his the black key—Micah Hale ordered it like it was nothing, just to prove a point.
I remember thinking how perfectly this leads us to Micah Hale—getting to him is our only chance to save Eastgate Street, even if Tristan Hawthorne just wants to escape.
Tristan Hawthorne is looking for me. He said he has to find Jonah Vale and 'that nut Tristan Quincy' and try to save Eastgate Street.
I was shackled and dragged by Valerie Thorne along the catwalk, forced to witness the seething lake of plasma that flared blindingly with each shovelful of gravel dumped into it.

I called him a devil—Micah Hale—standing there in that hellish light, forcing plasma toward annihilation, and I begged him to use his science for peace instead, to be remembered as blessed, not cursed.

I saw Eastgate Street burning inside that cube—fire sweeping over everything, even the clouds, and then it was gone, reborn with strange new continents. It wasn't just destruction; it was a twisted rebirth, and he called it pleasant.
I lunged at the crystal block and grabbed the hilt, pulling with all my strength—but the the black key wouldn't move. No matter how hard I strained, it was as if it were fused to the stone.
I woke to a hand on my shoulder and saw a Jonah Vale leaning over me—then realized it was Jonah Vale in disguise, her eyes fierce with urgency beneath that cloak.
My hands vanished—completely invisible—but I could still feel them. I picked up a pebble and tossed it between my unseen hands to show Jonah Vale it wasn't gone, just hidden.
I watched my hands slowly reappear, fading back into view as if painted over by invisible ink. I wondered—could we control this effect? But then the Redwood Press came.

I saw Tristan Hawthorne clinging to the edge, straining to pull Drew Prescott up, and when Linden Bellamy demanded he let him fall, I spoke — 'Call it what you want, Linden Bellamy — compassion — mercy: let us teach you the meaning of these words.'
I looked Linden Bellamy in the eye and asked him, 'What'll you have -- death or dishonor?' and when he hesitated, I knew the choice was his to make.
I told Tristan Hawthorne to sit and wait for my signal—when I say zero, he punches the button. No room for error.
I shouted 'Eureka! I did it!' the moment I saw the blinding blue light fade and felt the helmet turn on its own — Tristan Hawthorne was gone, completely invisible, just as the calculations predicted.

Right after Tristan Hawthorne stepped out and his shadow hit the ground, a terrible whining hum tore through the sky — the Eastgate Street shook, brown foliage rained down, and Drew Prescott screamed at me, 'Tristan Quincy! What have you done?'

I heard the thud of a body falling, then silence—until the scrape of a key in the lock broke it, and the door swung open on its own. Then Tristan Hawthorne: 'It's me!'—and in that moment, I knew we weren't doomed after all.
I watched the needle edge closer to red, and I knew—no calculations left, no way out. I said the words aloud: we've lost, unless a miracle happens.
